title: FBISE Annual Exam Simulator 01 (Book-II Prose & Heroes Section A)
subject: english-12

questions.question: According to Sir James Jeans in 'The Dying Sun', why is a rare occurrence for a star to come close to another star?

options.A: Stars travel in fixed magnetic orbits that keep them synchronized.
options.B: Space is so immense that a star travels millions of miles without meeting another, like a solitary ship on an ocean.
options.C: Stars possess gravitational repulsions that push oncoming bodies away.
options.D: Most stars are cold and do not radiate gravitational attraction.

questions.explanation: Sir James Jeans compares space to an immense ocean where each star is like a lonely ship traveling hundreds of thousands of miles without encountering another vessel.

questions.question: How does an educated scientific mind handle superstitions such as fear of the number 13 or black cats?

options.A: It rejects beliefs that have no empirical basis in cause-and-effect relationships.
options.B: It observes them secretly just in case luck plays a role.
options.C: It accepts them as ancient psychological wisdom.
options.D: It replaces them with astrological horoscopes.

questions.explanation: A person with a scientific attitude demands proven facts and logical causes before accepting any belief, rejecting baseless folklore and superstition.

questions.question: What sound symbolized the arrival of the weekend and boundless happiness for young Daiches?

options.A: The school brass bell clanging at 3:30 PM on Friday and the ringing of his bicycle bell
options.B: The church choir singing Sunday hymns
options.C: The sound of rain pouring on the roof on Saturday
options.D: The postman knocking on Saturday morning

questions.explanation: Walking out of school on Friday afternoon was pure ecstasy; the weekend felt like a blessed oasis of freedom.

questions.question: What emotional reaction did Squire feel right after hearing the splash of his sack sinking into the Thames?

options.A: Vicious vindictive laughter
options.B: A sudden pang of pity and pathos for the unfortunate, forgotten authors lying in cold mud
options.D: Desire to jump in and rescue them

questions.explanation: He felt a tender sadness imagining the ambitious poets and writers lying abandoned at the cold bottom of the river.

questions.question: Why did the bank manager usher Leacock into his private inner room with solemn secrecy?

options.A: He suspected Leacock was an international diamond smuggler.
options.B: Because Leacock whispered that he wished to speak with the manager 'alone', making him believe he was a Baron Rothschild or a Pinkerton detective.
options.C: Because the lobby was being renovated.
options.D: To offer him an executive vice-presidency.

questions.explanation: Leacock's mysterious, conspiratorial tone led the manager to assume he was an enormously wealthy capitalist or a private detective.

questions.question: In 'Hunger and Population Explosion', Anna McKenzie notes that a major historical cause of famine was:

options.A: Excessive production of synthetic fertilizers
options.B: Crop failure due to drought, floods, or blight, coupled with total lack of transport to bring food from surplus regions
options.D: Overpopulation of wild animals eating grains

questions.explanation: Famines historically occurred when weather destroyed crops and isolated communities had no mechanical transport to import grain.

questions.question: What unexpected academic advantage did Churchill gain by being placed in the lowest academic division at Harrow?

options.A: He was excused from all military drills.
options.B: While clever boys studied Latin and Greek, he was taught English language and grammar thoroughly by an exceptional teacher, Mr. Somervell.
options.C: He was permitted to leave school two years earlier.
options.D: He spent all his time playing polo.

questions.explanation: Because he was considered a dunce, Churchill had to master English grammar thoroughly—parsing sentences into color-coded parts—giving him command of prose.

questions.question: What nomadic Berber tribe inhabits the Hoggar mountains of the central Sahara, known as the 'Veiled Men' of the desert?

options.A: The Tuareg

questions.explanation: The Tuareg warriors wear indigo tagelmusts (face veils) covering their mouths and noses to protect against desert glare and sandstorms.

questions.question: Which Oxford University scientists successfully isolated, purified, and mass-produced Penicillin during the crisis of World War II?

options.A: Howard Florey and Ernst Chain

questions.explanation: Sir Howard Florey and Dr. Ernst Chain headed the Oxford research team that turned Fleming's raw mould juice into the miracle wonder drug.

questions.question: How did Pasteur attenuate (weaken) the rabies virus in his laboratory?

options.A: By drying infected spinal cords of rabbits in sterile dry air flasks for varying numbers of days
options.B: By boiling rabies tissue in carbolic acid
options.C: By exposing the virus to X-ray radiation
options.D: By freezing it in glacier ice

questions.explanation: Drying rabid rabbit spinal cords day by day systematically weakened the virus, allowing Pasteur to build immunity through progressively stronger doses.

questions.question: What treaty superseded the humiliating Treaty of Sèvres, establishing Turkey's modern sovereign borders in 1923?

options.A: The Treaty of Versailles

questions.explanation: The Treaty of Lausanne (July 1923) recognized total Turkish independence, abolishing the humiliating capitulations and foreign zones.

questions.question: What was Mustafa Kemal's famous national slogan advocating peaceful international diplomacy?

options.A: 'Conquer at all costs!'
options.B: 'Peace at home, peace in the world.' (Yurtta sulh, cihanda sulh)

questions.explanation: Kemal anchored Turkish foreign policy on peaceful coexistence, mutual respect of sovereignty, and regional non-aggression pacts.

questions.question: How did Chips first meet Katherine Bridges on the slopes of Great Gable?

options.A: He thought she was in mortal distress waving from a dangerous crag, rushed to rescue her, twisted his ankle, and she ended up rescuing him instead.
options.B: They met at a bicycle repair shop.
options.C: She was a guest at Brookfield chapel.
options.D: They collided on a railway platform.

questions.explanation: Chips saw her waving from a rock ledge, ran forward to help, slipped on loose scree, and sprained his ankle, leaving Katherine to nurse him.

questions.question: What was Katherine's attitude toward Chips' modest academic achievements?

options.A: She despised him for not having a first-class degree.
options.B: She loved him deeply for his honesty, gentle loyalty, quiet dignity, and genuine English steadfastness.
options.C: She forced him to study for a PhD in Paris.
options.D: She tried to make him leave education for business.

questions.explanation: Katherine saw behind his shy exterior to his profound goodness, gentle humor, and unwavering moral integrity.

questions.question: In 1908, when Chips turned sixty, what shocking demand did Ralston make during a private meeting in his study?

options.A: He bluntly demanded that Chips resign and retire immediately.
options.B: He offered Chips a salary increase.
options.C: He asked Chips to become head of the science department.
options.D: He requested Chips to paint the school chapel.

questions.explanation: Ralston summoned Chips and brutally told him that his methods were antiquated, his gown was tattered, and he was past his useful prime.

questions.question: In what year did Chips finally decide to retire peacefully from Brookfield due to a severe bout of bronchitis?

options.A: 1913, at the age of sixty-five

questions.explanation: Chips retired in July 1913, receiving a memorable farewell dinner and speech, moving across the road to Mrs. Wickett's house.

questions.question: What memorable words did young Linford say as he stepped out into the foggy dusk, echoing Katherine's words thirty-seven years earlier?

options.A: 'Good-bye, Mr. Chips!'

questions.explanation: As the boy waved through the mist, he called out: 'Good-bye, Mr. Chips!' bringing tears of nostalgic memory to Chips' eyes.

questions.question: What did Chips do with his modest financial savings in his last will and testament?

options.A: He left a portion to Mrs. Wickett and established an open scholarship fund for needy boys at Brookfield School.
options.B: He left everything to the British Treasury.
options.C: He bought gold bullion to bury in the woods.
options.D: He gave it all to foreign banks.

questions.explanation: Even in death, Chips ensured that his modest wealth benefited his loyal landlady and supported impoverished scholars at Brookfield.

questions.question: Choose the correct idiom meaning 'to face an unexpected, shocking calamity':

options.A: A bolt from the blue

questions.explanation: 'A bolt from the blue' describes a sudden, completely unexpected and shocking catastrophe.

questions.question: What is the meaning of the idiom 'to burn the candle at both ends'?

options.A: To light two candles during a blackout
options.B: To exhaust oneself by working late into the night and rising early, overtaxing one's physical energy

questions.explanation: Burning the candle at both ends means exhausting one's physical and mental resources through excessive, relentless labor.
